doc.title: Dick Hyman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Growing up in New York and seeing 52nd Street
summary: Rowe asks whether being born in New York mattered; Hyman says he could see many live players and get into studio work early.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: We are here today for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive and we have the great pleasure of talking with Mr. Dick Hyman, who has been described in a number of ways: eclectic, versatile, a Renaissance Man, and, I want to see if we can figure out when all that started and perhaps we’ll discuss why he’s called all those things. Do you think being born in New York City was important for your early —

For my being a Renaissance Man? Well, the fact that I was in New York did permit me to see a lot of people live when I was in my teens, and there was so much going on and there was still activity on 52nd street and in Greenwich Village. It was something that I guess people who grow up in Peoria don’t have. And then the fact also that I was able to get into studio work not too long after I began playing professionally, that was another thing that might not have happened to people who weren’t as fortunate as to be around New York.
